title: Articles and quantifiers
tagline: Small words, real difference: a/an/the/zero, and exactly how much of something there is.
exam: Reading & Use of English Part 2 — open cloze
Reading & Use of English Part 4 — key word transformations
Writing Part 2 — article or report: general claims vs specific examples
why: Articles and quantifiers are tiny words, but they change the meaning of a sentence completely: few friends helped and a few friends helped describe almost opposite situations. B2 First tests this precision directly in the open cloze, and it shows up in every piece of writing, where the wrong article can make a general idea sound oddly specific, or a specific one sound vague.

diagrams.title: a/an, the, or nothing at all?

rows.label: Used with
cells: a singular countable noun, first mention
something specific, known or unique
plural or uncountable nouns making a general statement

rows.label: Example
cells: Nadia joined a coding club.
The coding club meets on Fridays.
Coding clubs are popular in most schools.

rows.label: Key signal
cells: one example among many, not identified yet
already mentioned, obvious from context, or one of a kind
talking about the whole idea, not one example of it

rows.label: Common mistake
cells: forgetting it before a new countable noun
adding it to plural/uncountable nouns in general statements
adding it to unique or abstract nouns like 'space' or 'nature'

rows.label: Grammar
cells: each/every + singular noun + singular verb
all/both + plural noun + plural verb
neither/none of + singular verb (formal)

rows.label: Group size
cells: every = three or more; each = two or more
both = exactly two; all = three or more
neither = two; none = three or more

rows.label: Example
cells: Every student handed in the essay on time.
Both teams trained twice a week before the tournament.
Neither answer was completely correct.

rows.label: With 'of'
cells: each of + the/these + plural (never 'every of')
all of / both of + the + plural
none of + the + plural; neither of + the + two

head: Pattern
Rule
Example
rows: Zero article
plural or uncountable noun making a general statement
Music brings people together.
a/an
first mention of a singular countable noun
She joined a debate club last term.
the
something already known, unique or specified
The teacher who marked our essays retired.
the
superlatives and ranked or one-of-a-kind nouns
the most reliable Wi-Fi in the building
few / little
almost none — a negative idea; few + countable, little + uncountable
few volunteers turned up / little time left
a few / a little
some — a small, positive amount
a few good ideas / a little patience
plenty of / hardly any
more than enough / almost none; both work with countable and uncountable
plenty of practice tests / hardly any excuses
all / both / every / each / either / neither / none of
quantifying a defined group, not individuals
Neither team scored in the first half.

use.point: Choosing a/an, the or zero article for general, specific and abstract nouns

examples.text: Nadia is doing a research project on renewable energy this term.
examples.note: first mention, one example among many

examples.text: The project she chose looks at solar panels on school roofs.
Miss Vega says hard work matters more than natural talent.
examples.note: uncountable noun used generally, no article

use.point: Small or large amounts, countable and uncountable

examples.text: There were few empty seats left, so most of us had to stand.
Don't worry, there's a little time before the bus leaves.
examples.note: a little = a small but useful amount

examples.text: We only have a few days before the mock exam.

use.point: Talking about a whole group: all, both, every, each, neither, none

examples.text: Both teams trained twice a week before the tournament.
Neither of the two guides spoke English fluently.
None of the buses were running because of the strike.

use.point: In writing: general claims that sound natural, not translated

examples.text: Teenagers today spend too much time comparing themselves to influencers.
examples.note: general plural, zero article, common Part 2/Writing pattern

examples.text: The internet has changed how young people learn languages.
examples.note: the + specific technology, zero article + general group

watch_out.wrong: The teenagers today spend too much time online.
watch_out.right: Teenagers today spend too much time online.
watch_out.why: A general statement about a whole group of people never takes the.

watch_out.wrong: She gave me an advice about the interview.
watch_out.right: She gave me some advice about the interview.
watch_out.why: Advice is uncountable, so it can't take a/an; use some or leave it bare.

watch_out.wrong: Sofia has read less books this term than Nadia.
watch_out.right: Sofia has read fewer books this term than Nadia.
watch_out.why: Fewer goes with countable nouns like books; less is for uncountable nouns.

watch_out.wrong: There's little snacks left, so let's share.
watch_out.right: There are a few snacks left, so let's share.
watch_out.why: Little is for uncountable nouns; snacks is countable and plural, so it needs a few + plural verb.

watch_out.wrong: Every of the students passed the mock exam.
watch_out.right: Every one of the students passed the mock exam.
watch_out.why: Every is never followed directly by of; use every one of or switch to all of / each of.

watch_out.wrong: None of the two answers was correct.
watch_out.right: Neither of the two answers was correct.
watch_out.why: None of is for three or more; with exactly two, use neither.

dialogue.title: Planning the coastal clean-up
dialogue.context: Mateo, Sofia and Liam are organising a beach clean-up on the coast for their environmental club, and Miss Vega stops by to check on the plan.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: So far only a few people have signed up. We need more volunteers.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: That's the problem with posting it online — few students actually read the group chat.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: Let's ask Miss Vega if we can announce it in class. The whole point is getting more hands on the beach.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Good idea. How much rubbish are we talking about, roughly?

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: Plenty of it, unfortunately — plastic bottles mostly, and hardly any bins nearby.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: And equipment? Do we have enough gloves and bags for everyone?

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: We've got a little money left from the last fundraiser, so we can buy more if we need to.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: Every student who comes should bring their own water bottle, though — no plastic ones.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Sensible. And Nadia mentioned both her cousins want to help too.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: Great — that's a few more names on the list, then.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: None of this works without transport, though. Can the school arrange a bus?

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Leave that with me. If enough of you turn up on Saturday, I'll sort out the rest.

items.sentence: ___ moon looked enormous over the Andes last night.
items.why: there is only one moon, so it's unique — use 'the'

items.sentence: Mateo says ___ honesty matters more than talent in football.
items.why: uncountable abstract noun in a general statement → zero article

items.sentence: There were ___ empty seats left, so most of us had to stand.
items.why: 'few' = almost none, matching the negative idea of having to stand

items.sentence: Don't worry, there's ___ time before the bus leaves — we can grab a snack.
items.why: 'a little' = a small but useful amount, a positive idea here

items.sentence: ___ of the two teams scored, so the match finished nil-nil.
items.why: 'neither' is for exactly two; 'none' would be used for three or more

items.sentence: Sofia has read ___ books this term than Nadia has.
items.why: 'fewer' goes with the countable noun 'books'; 'less' is for uncountable nouns

practice.instructions: Complete each sentence with a suitable article or quantifier.

items.sentence: Nadia is doing ___ research project on renewable energy this term.
___ information Miss Vega gave us about the trip was really useful.
There's ___ point complaining if we don't email the organisers ourselves.
We only have ___ days before the mock exam, so we need a revision timetable.
___ of the two guides spoke English fluently, so we used a translation app.
___ single student in the group contributed something different to the poster.
That's ___ best essay Sofia has written so far this year.

practice.instructions: Complete the second sentence so that it has a similar meaning to the first. Use the word given. Do not change it. Use between two and five words.

items.first: Hardly any of my classmates brought umbrellas today.
items.second_end: of my classmates brought umbrellas today.

items.first: There was more than enough food for everyone at the festival.
items.second_end: food for everyone at the festival.

items.first: The teacher gave every student a separate rubric.
The two restaurants were both closed on Sunday.
Every single member of the choir turned up for rehearsal.

summary: Use a/an for a first mention, the for something specific or unique, and no article for general plural or uncountable nouns.
Few and little suggest almost none; a few and a little suggest a small but real amount.
Each and every take a singular noun and verb; all and both take a plural noun and verb.
Neither and none of both mean 'not one', but neither is only for two.
In open cloze and in your own writing, check whether the noun is general or specific before choosing the article.
